n: Matthew opens his Gospel by presenting Jesus’s family line. Writing especially for Jewish readers, he shows that Jesus is the heir of the two great covenants: the royal promise to David and the blessing promised to Abraham.

f.g: Genealogy, origin — the Greek word is genesis.

n: The line begins with the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. “Judas” is the Greek form of Judah, the son through whom the royal line would come.

f.g: Judah, son of Jacob — Greek forms of Old Testament names are used throughout.
Fathered, or became ancestor of.

n: Matthew unusually includes women. Tamar, a Canaanite widow, bore twins to Judah after a troubled episode. Including her shows God working through imperfect family stories.

f.g: Perez and Zerah, Judah’s twin sons.
Hezron.

n: The list continues through the generations in Egypt and the wilderness. Nahshon was the leader of Judah’s tribe in Moses’s day.

f.g: Ram (1 Chronicles 2:9-10).
Nahshon, Aaron’s brother-in-law.

n: Two more remarkable women: Rahab, the Canaanite of Jericho who protected Israel’s spies, and Ruth, the Moabite who chose Israel’s God. Gentile women are part of the Messiah’s heritage.

f.g: Rahab.
Boaz.

n: David becomes king. Matthew pointedly calls Bathsheba “the wife of Uriah,” recalling David’s sin — and God’s grace in continuing the line through Solomon.

f.w: her that had been the wife of Urias

n: After Solomon come the kings of Judah: Rehoboam, Abijah, and Asa.

f.g: Rehoboam, under whom the kingdom split.
Abijah (Abijam).

n: Next are Jehoshaphat, Jehoram, and Uzziah. Matthew skips three kings between Jehoram and Uzziah — ancient genealogies often abbreviated to make a pattern.

f.g: Jehoshaphat, a righteous king.
Uzziah — Matthew omits Ahaziah, Joash, and Amaziah.

n: Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah — kings during Isaiah’s ministry.

f.g: Ahaz.
Hezekiah.

n: Manasseh, the most wicked king, who later repented; then Amon and the righteous reformer Josiah.

f.g: Josiah.

n: The Babylonian exile interrupts the royal line. “Jechonias” is Jehoiachin, actually Josiah’s grandson. The line of kings seems to end in disaster.

f.g: Jeconiah, also called Jehoiachin or Coniah.

n: Yet the line continues in exile. Zerubbabel, Jehoiachin’s grandson, led the return from Babylon and rebuilt the temple.

f.g: Shealtiel.
Zerubbabel, governor of Judah.

n: From here the names aren’t found in the Old Testament; Matthew likely drew on family or public records. David’s descendants lived as ordinary people for centuries.

f.g: This and the following names appear only here.

n: More generations pass in obscurity, yet God preserved the line.

f.g: Zadok — not the famous priest of David’s time.

n: The list approaches Joseph. Luke 3 gives a different genealogy, which many explain as Mary’s line or a legal versus biological line.
Matthew carefully changes the pattern: Joseph is “the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus.” Joseph was Jesus’s legal father, giving Him a royal claim, but Jesus was not his biological son.

f.g: Greek Christos, “Anointed One” — the same meaning as the Hebrew Messiah.

n: Matthew arranges the history into three sets of fourteen generations. Fourteen may echo David’s name, whose Hebrew letters add up to fourteen. History moves according to God’s plan toward Christ.

f.g: The Hebrew letters of David (D-W-D) have numeric values 4+6+4 = 14.

n: Mary was betrothed (legally pledged) to Joseph, but before they lived together she was found to be pregnant by the power of the Holy Ghost.

f.g: Betrothed — a binding engagement, legally like marriage, before the couple lived together.

f.w: with child of the Holy Ghost

n: Joseph, a righteous man, didn’t want to shame Mary publicly, so he planned to end the betrothal quietly. His goodness shows both obedience to the law and mercy.

f.g: Righteous, upright.
Divorce her privately; ending a betrothal required a divorce.

n: As Joseph considered this, an angel came in a dream: “Joseph, son of David, don’t be afraid to take Mary as your wife; the child is from the Holy Ghost.” God guides Joseph through dreams, like the Joseph of Genesis.

f.g: A reminder of Joseph’s royal lineage, passed legally to Jesus.

n: Mary will have a son, and Joseph is to name Him Jesus, for He will save His people from their sins. The name itself declares His mission.

f.g: Greek form of Joshua (Yehoshua), meaning “Jehovah saves.”

f.w: he shall save his people from their sins

n: Matthew often notes how events fulfill prophecy — about a dozen times. This is the first.

f.g: A key phrase in Matthew, connecting Jesus to Old Testament prophecy.

n: Matthew quotes Isaiah: a virgin will bear a son called Emmanuel, “God with us.” In Jesus, God Himself came to live among His people.

f.w: Behold, a virgin shall be with child

f.g: Hebrew Immanu-El, “God with us.”

n: Joseph woke up and obeyed immediately, taking Mary as his wife. His quiet faith is an example of trusting revelation.

f.w: did as the angel of the Lord had bidden him

n: Joseph did not have marital relations with Mary until after Jesus’s birth, confirming the virgin birth. He named the child Jesus, as commanded, accepting Him as his legal son.

f.g: Did not have marital relations with her.
